head.citation-title: Enhancing carbon storage potential and performance of concrete: Synergy of waste paper ash incorporation and accelerated carbonation curing
head.abstracts: © 2026 The Authors.This paper examines the use of waste paper ash (WPA) as a partial cement substitute, combined with accelerated carbonation curing, to mitigate the CO2 impact associated with concrete production. The chemical, physical, and microstructural properties of the WPA were investigated. Then, the effect of WPA replacement levels (5, 10, and 20%), aggregate-to-binder ratio (5, 6, and 7), water-to-binder ratio (0.45, 0.50, and 0.55), and carbonation curing durations (4, 8, and 20 h) on the performance of concrete were evaluated, including CO2 uptake, compressive strength, permeable pores, and water absorption. The Taguchi optimization method was employed to maximize CO2 sequestration in blended carbonation-cured concrete. The experimental results suggested that the optimum mix, consisting of a WPA replacement of 10%, an aggregate-to-binder ratio of 5, a water-to-binder ratio of 0.55, and 8 h of carbonation, had a CO2 uptake of 16.4%, a 28-day compressive strength of 19.4 MPa, water absorption of 6.5%, and volume of permeable voids of 22.9%. Furthermore, X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) of the optimum mix highlighted the synergic formation of carbonation and hydration products, including calcium carbonate and calcium silicate hydrate, respectively. This study provides insight into a blended carbonation-cured concrete containing WPA, while contributing to the decarbonization of the concrete sector and the circular economy.

coredata.dc:description: This paper examines the use of waste paper ash (WPA) as a partial cement substitute, combined with accelerated carbonation curing, to mitigate the CO2 impact associated with concrete production. The chemical, physical, and microstructural properties of the WPA were investigated. Then, the effect of WPA replacement levels (5, 10, and 20%), aggregate-to-binder ratio (5, 6, and 7), water-to-binder ratio (0.45, 0.50, and 0.55), and carbonation curing durations (4, 8, and 20 h) on the performance of concrete were evaluated, including CO2 uptake, compressive strength, permeable pores, and water absorption. The Taguchi optimization method was employed to maximize CO2 sequestration in blended carbonation-cured concrete. The experimental results suggested that the optimum mix, consisting of a WPA replacement of 10%, an aggregate-to-binder ratio of 5, a water-to-binder ratio of 0.55, and 8 h of carbonation, had a CO2 uptake of 16.4%, a 28-day compressive strength of 19.4 MPa, water absorption of 6.5%, and volume of permeable voids of 22.9%. Furthermore, X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) of the optimum mix highlighted the synergic formation of carbonation and hydration products, including calcium carbonate and calcium silicate hydrate, respectively. This study provides insight into a blended carbonation-cured concrete containing WPA, while contributing to the decarbonization of the concrete sector and the circular economy.
coredata.dc:title: Enhancing carbon storage potential and performance of concrete: Synergy of waste paper ash incorporation and accelerated carbonation curing
